Causative get and have
You use a causative verb when you want to talk about something that someone else did for you or for another person.
The subject caused the action to happen, but didn't do it themselves.
To have someone do something

You use the form:
subject + have + person + infinitive

Here are some examples:
I had my husband make a list of all the things that needed to be fixed around the house.
The women had her daughter wash the dishes and sweep the floor.
To get someone to do something

You use the form:
get + someone + to + infinitive

Here are some examples:
The parents get their children to complete a list of chores before they are allowed to watch television.
I get my neighbor to help me clean the driveway.
Once, a friend of mine had her husband look after their house for two weeks while she went on holidays.
Have him choose three chores to do for the week to start with.
Make a list of all the weekly household chores you complete and then get him to read it.
Be Supposed To
You use the structure be supposed to when you want to talk about expectations, obligations or arrangements.
You can use be supposed to to talk about situations in the past, present or future.

The structure is:

Subject + To be + supposed to + verb

Present: I am supposed to clean the house today.
Past: I was supposed to take out the trash last night.
Future: I am supposed to collect my dry cleaning tomorrow.

**Pronunciation tip**:
When you say be supposed to, you link the /d/ and /t/ sounds together.

Like this:
Be suppose_to
Was/were going to
You use the future in the past to express the idea that in the past you thought something would happen in the future. It does not matter if you are correct or not.

Example:
We were going to take an equal share in the household chores.
He was supposed to take out the trash this morning for collection but instead he slept in.
He promised me that he was going to clean up the “man cave” the next morning.
If the two of you are going to have a successful marriage, you need to be on the same page.

images.text:
Dear Sally,
I really need some advice. My husband and I were recently married. I have come to realize that he is oblivious to the amount of housework needed to maintain a home. I have a feeling that he would get his mother to cook, clean and wash for him. I'm sure he never lifted a finger. He was supposed to take out the trash this morning for collection but instead he slept in.

Last weekend, a group of his friends came over for pizza and to watch the hockey game. He promised me that he was going to clean up the “man cave” the next morning. Needless to say, I spent almost an hour vacuuming the carpet, collecting bottles and trying to get the stains out of the lounge suite. He was nowhere to be seen. I thought marriage was supposed to be an equal partnership. Right now, I'm getting the raw end of the deal.
Bitter and Confused

Dear Bitter and Confused,
I'm sorry to hear that your husband isn't pulling his weight around the house. My advice would be to sit down and have a frank discussion about your concerns. He needs to realize that he has responsibilities. Make a list of all the weekly household chores you complete and then get him to read it. Have him choose three chores to do for the week to start with. Once, a friend of mine had her husband look after their house for two weeks while she went on holidays. He quickly understood the error of his ways. If the two of you are going to have a successful marriage, you need to be on the same page.
Sally
